title: Gradual state sync strategy for on‑prem control-plane migration
content:
Purpose and scope:
This doc captures a pragmatic, low-risk approach for migrating customer on‑prem control planes (and the associated runtime state) from the legacy control plane implementation (v1) to the new control plane (v2) with minimal disruption. Focus is on designs for gradual state synchronization, consistency guarantees, Terraform considerations for state and lock migration, telemetry gating, and an explicit, testable rollback plan.

Context and constraints (quick notes):
- Many private deployments run with restricted network connectivity and ops windows.
- We cannot assume a single moment cutover: customers expect low/no downtime and local compliance requirements sometimes prevent opening cross-region channels.
- Legacy control plane stores runtime metadata in a persisted KV store (etcd v3 backing) and also stores derived caches in a Redis cluster.
- New control plane (v2) uses a sharded, versioned keyspace and a migration-compatible schema but needs a canonical sync window to converge.

High-level strategy (three lanes):
1) Passive shadow sync (read-only replication to v2): replicate all writes from v1 -> v2 asynchronously, but answer reads from v1. This lets v2 populate its KV without serving primary traffic.
2) Dual-write with probabilistic verification (canary phase): route a small % of customer read/write traffic to v2 in dual-write mode. v2 writes live, v1 continues as source-of-truth. Compare results, run reconciliation jobs on mismatches.
3) Controlled promotion: after canaries pass and reconciliation lag is within threshold, promote v2 to primary for an increasing set of routes/pods. Maintain read‑fallback to v1 for a conservative fallback window.

State sync mechanics and components:
- CDC pipeline: use a lightweight change-data-capture component to tail v1’s write-ahead log (or etcd watch stream) and emit idempotent events to a migration topic (Kafka or a buffered S3 staging for air-gapped sites).
- Transformer: events are translated into the v2 key format and annotated with a version vector and source timestamp. Keep transformation logic small to avoid semantic drift.
- Idempotency: every write to v2 must be idempotent (use write token + last-modified) to support retries.
- Reconciliation service: periodic full-key diffs for hot prefixes (e.g., active deployments, model pins, routing tables) and sampling diffs for cold keys. Maintain per-customer reconciliation deltas.
- TTLs and derived caches: do not attempt to migrate ephemeral caches directly — instead, seed cache warmers on v2 and allow caches to rehydrate.

Edge cases and consistency model:
- Accept eventual consistency during initial phases.
- For strong-consistency operations (billing events, admin write locks), gate them: route those operations through a safe RPC to v1 until the customer opts into the v2 control-plane feature flag.
- Detect and avoid write skew: for concurrent updates that rely on read-modify-write semantics, use compare-and-swap semantics in the transformer where supported; otherwise degrade to single-transaction proxying through v1.

Terraform / IaC notes and gotchas:
- Remote state backend: ensure remote tfstate is exported and verified before any control-plane change. If customer uses local state, coordinate manual export with infra owner.
- Provider lock: bump provider versions in a separate PR and run plan-only in staging; do not apply provider upgrades at the same time as state migration.
- Resource ID mapping: v2 may introduce changed resource IDs (e.g., controlplane_cluster -> cp_cluster_v2). Provide a migration mapping file and a small wrapper script: terraform state mv old.resource new.resource — but do this only for non-sensitive resources.
- Locking and apply sequencing: use an operator-controlled apply gate. Sequence: (1) export state, (2) plan with new module, (3) dry-run apply to a shadow workspace, (4) apply to production workspace with watch and locks.
- Example snippet we used during lab: 
  - terraform workspace new-migration-shadow
  - terraform init -backend-config='bucket=redwood-migrations'
  - terraform plan -out=mig.plan
  - terraform apply "mig.plan"
- Secrets / KMS: ensure v2 has KMS access to decrypt any secrets needed during bootstrap. If using HSM in-customer, coordinate key rotation windows separately.

Canary & traffic routing policy (practical checklist):
- Canary targets: choose low-risk tenants (internal tests + 2 customers with active dev traffic).
- Traffic split: start 1% writes, 100% reads still via v1 (passive shadow). Gradually increase dual-write to 5% then 20% over multiple days depending on metrics.
- Read fallback: implement read-with-fallback for N seconds — if v2 read fails or returns stale version (older than TTL) then fallback to v1. Log fallback reasons.
- Fallback metric: per-minute fallback-rate < 0.1% before wider promotion.

Telemetry and SLO gates (Prometheus examples + thresholds):
- Key metrics to track:
  - migration.reconciler.lag_seconds (median, p95) -> target: median < 3s, p95 < 30s for hot keys
  - migration.write_failure_rate (per 1000 writes) -> target: < 1 failure per 10k in canary
  - controlplane.api_error_rate (v2) -> target: < 0.5% during canary
  - fallback.rate (reads falling back to v1) -> target: < 0.1%
  - reconciliation.mismatch_ratio -> target: < 0.01 for canary tenants
- Alerting rules (examples):
  - ALERT MigrationLagHigh IF migration_reconciler_lag_seconds_p95 > 120 FOR 5m
  - ALERT DualWriteErrors IF increase(migration_write_failure_rate[5m]) > 0.05
- Dashboards: per-tenant reconciliation panel, per-shard lag, last-successful-sync timestamp.

Reconciliation policies and automated healing:
- Two levels: fast (per-key sampling every 1m for hot keys) and slow (full-key scan for customer every 24h).
- Auto-repair: for mismatches under age threshold (e.g., < 1h), prefer v1 canonical value and overwrite v2; for mismatches > 7d, issue manual review ticket and pause auto-repair for that tenant.
- Conflict resolution strategy documented for three cases: newer-timestamp-wins (default), OR merge-by-type (list-appends), OR admin-resolve for opaque blobs.

Rollback playbook (explicit):
1) Abort canary: disable routing rules that send writes to v2 and switch new requests back to v1.
2) Stop CDC: pause the CDC pipeline so v2 stops receiving new events.
3) Reconcile immediate divergence: run a targeted reconciliation for canary tenants and reapply missing writes to v1 if any were inadvertently promoted.
4) Drain v2 writers: mark v2 as read-only for all critical keys; leave read fallback intact.
5) Terraform state backout: if any tfstate moved, use terraform state mv to map resource IDs back, and run a plan to verify parity.
6) Postmortem triggers: automatically create a PAG ticket and assign the migration owner if mismatch_ratio > threshold or fallback spikes.

Operational runbook checklist (pre-migration):
- [ ] Confirm change window and customer ops contact list present.
- [ ] Export and verify tfstate; store in migration bucket with immutability flag for 48h.
- [ ] Smoke tests for critical APIs on staging v2 (create/delete/lock/unlock).
- [ ] End-to-end test run (including billing writes) against a staging mirror.
- [ ] Verify KMS/HSM access from v2 nodes.
- [ ] Wire up reconciliation alerts to oncall and to the migration channel in Slack.

Rollback checklist (if needed):
- [ ] Stop canary writes by flipping routing rule
- [ ] Resume v1-only traffic and set v2 to read-only for critical keys
- [ ] Run immediate reconciliation for canary tenants
- [ ] Execute tfstate reconciliation scripts (terraform state list -> validate)
- [ ] Notify affected customers and publish short incident update

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self):
- How to best handle tenants with on-prem Redis clusters behind NAT? (short-term: use a local agent to perform rewrites; long-term: design a brokered sync.)
- Should we add a vector clock per key to avoid relying only on wall-clock timestamps? Discuss with applied-ml for performance impact.
- Validate the cost of keeping CDC topic storage for 30 days for replay during postmortem vs snapshot exports.
- Write migration “canary playbook” script that automates the sequence: enable-cdc -> seed -> dual-write -> sample-diff -> promote.

Appendix: quick commands and snippets used in dry runs:
- Start CDC (kafka-based): 
  ./migration-agent --src etcd://v1:2379 --sink kafka://migrate-topic --transform transform.js &
- Run reconciliation job for tenant foo-corp:
  python3 tools/reconcile.py --tenant foo-corp --sample hot --fix --dry-run
- Terraform sample: 
  terraform workspace select prod
  terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars -out=prod.plan
  terraform apply "prod.plan"

Final notes:
This doc is intentionally prescriptive but conservative. The migration can be shortened for trusted customers, but the recommended default is the three-lane approach above. Next step: pair with SRE to produce an automated canary runner and finalize the reconciliation repair rules.

Tagged owners: migration lead = Sofia Martinez; infra owner = Ravi Patel; telemetry = Evelyn Cho

End of doc (draft).
